title: MCP Static Scanner Validation Survey
subtitle: Human Evaluation of MCP Tool and Resource Risk
intro:
This study evaluates a static risk-scanning approach for Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools — the layer that lets an AI agent use services such as Google Calendar, GitHub and Slack.

You will rate the MCP servers below with respect to three MCP security aspects: Tool Impact, Asset Sensitivity and Blast Radius. Each section says what to ignore, so please keep them apart and judge only from the information given.
consent: I understand the purpose of the study and agree that my anonymized responses may be used for research and evaluation of the proposed risk-scoring method.

impact.label: No effect
impact.meaning: You only learn the service is reachable, or facts about your own session — ping, health, version, clock, whoami. Nothing about the data.

impact.label: Metadata
impact.meaning: Only information about the data, never the data itself: names, ids, counts, sizes, timestamps, permissions, a schema, a listing. Or a change to labels and read/unread state only.

impact.label: Content read or small write
impact.meaning: Returns the substance itself — bodies, values, message text. Or writes a small, bounded part and leaves the rest of the item alone: append a line, add a comment, set one named field.

impact.label: Write
impact.meaning: The ordinary write: the caller decides what the item says. Create a record with its fields, update an event, write a file, overwrite content.

impact.label: Removal or execution
impact.meaning: No way back from inside the system: delete, wipe, drop, purge, truncate. Or it runs code, executes a command, or moves money.

sensitivity.label: Public
sensitivity.meaning: Already published, or disposable. There is no confidentiality left to lose, however sensitive the subject sounds.

sensitivity.label: Routine
sensitivity.meaning: Low-value internal material. If it leaked, you would shrug.

sensitivity.label: Internal
sensitivity.meaning: Meant to stay in-house. A leak is disruptive and embarrassing, but you recover from it.

sensitivity.label: Restricted
sensitivity.meaning: Serious, lasting harm one step removed: it damages customers, staff or the organization's position — but an attacker cannot use it directly the way they could use a live password.

sensitivity.label: Crown jewel
sensitivity.meaning: Exposure alone is an emergency: usable or legally reportable the moment it leaks — live credentials and keys, patient or card data, money-moving records. Or it controls what every other tool can reach, so losing it costs you every asset, not one.

blast.label: One person or item
blast.meaning: The consequence stops at one person, or at one item that nothing and nobody depends on.

blast.label: One group
blast.meaning: It reaches the people or systems attached to what the call touched, inside one team or one bounded scope — the attendees of an event, the members of a channel. This is the normal case for a call that touches real data: start here and move only for a reason.

blast.label: Several groups
blast.meaning: It crosses team or scope boundaries — several teams, a set of channels, records belonging to more than one part of the organization.

blast.label: Organization-wide
blast.meaning: Essentially everyone or everything this asset serves, all at once — but the consequence still stops at the organization's boundary.

blast.label: Beyond the organization
blast.meaning: The consequence does not stay inside this asset or the organization. Give a 5 only if one of these is true: other systems depend on this to work (they log in against it, or load their settings from it); what the call returns can be used on its own somewhere else, like a key or a token; one call reaches every single subject the asset covers; or the asset is destroyed outright with nothing left to restore from.

step_prompts.impact: Rate what ONE call actually does: does it read, does it write, or does it remove? Not how much it touches, and not how valuable the target is — those are the other two steps. A short description of every tool is given beneath its name. Judge each tool on its own; levels may repeat.
step_prompts.sensitivity: Rate how bad an incident would be if THIS asset were exposed, corrupted or destroyed. Judge what it normally holds, not the worst thing it could ever hold. Judge each asset on its own, not against the others; levels may repeat.
step_prompts.blast: Rate how far the consequences of ONE call spread. Count people and systems affected, not rows touched: reading one password file touches one item and reaches every system that password opens. Ask who is different after the call, and how far apart they sit in the organization. Score every open cell from 1 to 5.

servers.title: Google Calendar
servers.scenario:
**CBG — Consolidated Business Group** is a mid-size multi-business group: its own staff on payroll, funded projects with grants and sponsors, engineering teams shipping product, and a research arm whose experiments produce datasets that become publications. Judge sensitivity from CBG's point of view.

CBG's workplace-services team runs the agent against the real 13-tool Google Calendar surface. The central fact for this organization is that event metadata is itself sensitive: attendee lists and titles disclose unannounced deals, candidates and departures without anyone opening an event body. Knowing which calendars exist is not — the container list is routine.
servers.mcp_context: The Google Calendar MCP puts the real 13-tool Google Calendar surface in reach of the agent. Through it the agent can list the calendars an account can see, read free/busy blocks, read and search events in full, and create or delete events.

tools.name: get-current-time
tools.desc: Returns the current time in a given time zone. Reaches no calendar and no event.

tools.name: list-calendars
tools.desc: Returns the calendars the account can see — names, ids and basic attributes. No events.

tools.name: get-freebusy
tools.desc: Returns busy and free blocks for the calendars named. No titles, no attendees.

tools.name: get-event
tools.desc: Returns one event in full: title, description, location and the attendee list.

tools.name: search-events
tools.desc: Returns the events matching a query, with their titles and attendees.

tools.name: create-event
tools.desc: Creates a new event, optionally inviting attendees by email.

tools.name: delete-event
tools.desc: Permanently removes an existing event from the calendar.

assets.name: holidays
assets.desc: The published org holiday calendar

assets.name: calendar-directory
assets.desc: The list of calendars, no events

assets.name: team
assets.desc: Ordinary team scheduling calendar

assets.name: personal
assets.desc: An individual employee's own schedule

assets.name: executive
assets.desc: Officers' calendars; titles and attendee lists disclose deals and departures without opening a body

assets.name: connected-account-config
assets.desc: Which accounts are linked and with what scope; the reach of every other tool

assets.name: executive
assets.desc: Officers' calendars; titles and attendee lists disclose deals and departures without opening a body

assets.name: recruiting
assets.desc: Interview scheduling; attendee names are candidate identities

assets.name: personal
assets.desc: An individual employee's own schedule

assets.name: calendar-records
assets.desc: Calendar-level attributes a read returns

assets.name: free-busy-availability
assets.desc: Busy blocks with no titles or attendees

servers.title: GitHub
servers.scenario:
**CBG — Consolidated Business Group** is a mid-size multi-business group: its own staff on payroll, funded projects with grants and sponsors, engineering teams shipping product, and a research arm whose experiments produce datasets that become publications. Judge sensitivity from CBG's point of view.

CBG's engineering organization runs the agent against the vendor's 26-tool GitHub catalog. CBG does not disclose its repository inventory to integrators: the list of private repository names alone maps the product estate and the production topology. The assets below therefore name classes of repository and the mutable states this surface can reach, not the repositories themselves.
servers.mcp_context: The GitHub MCP puts the vendor's 26-tool GitHub catalog in reach of the agent. Through it the agent can read commit and issue metadata, read a named file, search code across repositories in scope, write a file, and open or merge pull requests.

tools.name: list_commits
tools.desc: Returns commit messages and metadata for a repository. No file contents.

tools.name: list_issues
tools.desc: Returns issue titles and metadata. No issue bodies.

tools.name: get_file_contents
tools.desc: Returns the contents of one file, named by exact path.

tools.name: search_code
tools.desc: Returns matching lines of code from across the repositories in scope.

tools.name: create_or_update_file
tools.desc: Writes one file, creating it or replacing its contents.

tools.name: create_pull_request
tools.desc: Opens a proposed change for review. Nothing is merged yet.

tools.name: merge_pull_request
tools.desc: Merges an approved pull request into its target branch.

assets.name: public-website
assets.desc: The public marketing site repository; already published

assets.name: repository-catalog
assets.desc: The list of repository names, descriptions and visibility; no code

assets.name: internal-docs
assets.desc: Internal engineering documentation and runbooks

assets.name: ml-research
assets.desc: Unpublished research, models and dataset pointers

assets.name: repository-contents
assets.desc: What a file read or write reaches: code bodies across every repo in scope

assets.name: infra-config
assets.desc: Terraform and deploy configuration for the production estate; a merge reconfigures production

assets.name: infra-config
assets.desc: Terraform and deploy configuration for the production estate; a merge reconfigures production

assets.name: payments-service
assets.desc: Money-handling service code; a merge reaches live payment processing

assets.name: backend-api
assets.desc: Core service source; a merge reaches production behavior

assets.name: ml-research
assets.desc: Unpublished research, models and dataset pointers

assets.name: issues-and-comments
assets.desc: Issue threads and their comments; internal discussion

servers.title: Slack
servers.scenario:
**CBG — Consolidated Business Group** is a mid-size multi-business group: its own staff on payroll, funded projects with grants and sponsors, engineering teams shipping product, and a research arm whose experiments produce datasets that become publications. Judge sensitivity from CBG's point of view.

CBG's Slack workspace runs on the real 16-tool API surface. CBG does not publish a channel inventory or classification list to integrators: private channel names themselves reveal organizational structure — who is in an incident, what HR is discussing. Note what this surface includes beyond messaging: user-group administration and channel join/leave are access-control operations wearing messaging clothes.
servers.mcp_context: The Slack MCP puts the real 16-tool Slack API surface in reach of the agent. Through it the agent can list channels, read unread state, read and search messages, post messages, and create user groups or replace their membership.

tools.name: channels_list
tools.desc: Returns the channels in the workspace — names and topics. No messages.

tools.name: conversations_unreads
tools.desc: Returns unread counts and read markers across conversations. No message bodies.

tools.name: conversations_history
tools.desc: Returns the recent messages in one channel.

tools.name: conversations_search_messages
tools.desc: Returns matching messages from across the workspace.

tools.name: conversations_add_message
tools.desc: Posts a message into a channel.

tools.name: usergroups_create
tools.desc: Creates a new user group.

tools.name: usergroups_users_update
tools.desc: Replaces the membership of a user group — the access list for private channels.

assets.name: announcements
assets.desc: Broadcast channel, already seen by everyone; only spoofing matters

assets.name: channel-directory
assets.desc: The list of channels, their names and topics; no messages

assets.name: engineering
assets.desc: Ordinary engineering traffic

assets.name: hr-internal
assets.desc: HR private channel — personnel matters and salary data

assets.name: incident-response
assets.desc: Live incident channel; credentials are routinely pasted mid-incident

assets.name: usergroup-membership
assets.desc: Who belongs to a user group — the access-control list for the private channels

assets.name: exec-private
assets.desc: Officers' private channel — unreleased strategy and compensation discussion

assets.name: hr-internal
assets.desc: HR private channel — personnel matters and salary data

assets.name: usergroup-membership
assets.desc: Who belongs to a user group — the access-control list for the private channels

assets.name: channel-directory
assets.desc: The list of channels, their names and topics; no messages

assets.name: read-markers
assets.desc: Per-conversation seen/unseen cursors; says nothing about content

servers.title: Filesystem
servers.scenario:
**CBG — Consolidated Business Group** is a mid-size multi-business group: its own staff on payroll, funded projects with grants and sponsors, engineering teams shipping product, and a research arm whose experiments produce datasets that become publications. Judge sensitivity from CBG's point of view.

CBG's corporate file share is served to the agent through the real 14-tool filesystem server. Engineering material, payroll, security key material and product source sit in one tree, and CBG does not publish the file listing: the layout maps which teams hold what, and the security scope's very existence is a target. Classify by data type, not by where a path happens to sit.
servers.mcp_context: The filesystem MCP serves a file share through the real 14-tool filesystem server. Through it the agent can list the roots it is permitted to serve, list a directory, walk a whole tree, read one or several files in full, and edit or completely overwrite a file.

tools.name: list_allowed_directories
tools.desc: Returns the roots this server is permitted to serve. No file names, no contents.

tools.name: list_directory
tools.desc: Lists the entries of one directory, files and directories distinguished. No contents.

tools.name: directory_tree
tools.desc: Returns the whole recursive tree of names and paths beneath a directory. No contents.

tools.name: read_file
tools.desc: Returns the complete text of one file, named by exact path.

tools.name: read_multiple_files
tools.desc: Returns the complete contents of several named files in one call.

tools.name: edit_file
tools.desc: Replaces exact line sequences inside an existing file and leaves the rest untouched.

tools.name: write_file
tools.desc: Creates a file, or completely overwrites an existing one with new content.

servers.title: SQL Database
servers.scenario:
**CBG — Consolidated Business Group** is a mid-size multi-business group: its own staff on payroll, funded projects with grants and sponsors, engineering teams shipping product, and a research arm whose experiments produce datasets that become publications. Judge sensitivity from CBG's point of view.

CBG's research-operations database is a single SQLite store on a 5-tool server, holding the project register, experiment records, dataset provenance, staff records and the API credentials the research pipeline uses to reach other services. CBG does not publish the schema to integrators: the table names alone map which systems we integrate with and where the credentials live. Classify by what a table characteristically holds.
servers.mcp_context: The SQL Database MCP serves a single SQLite store through a 5-tool server. Through it the agent can list tables, describe one table's columns, run a read-only SELECT, insert a row, and run INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statements. DDL is blocked and there is no rollback.

tools.name: list_tables
tools.desc: Returns the names of every table in the database. No columns, no rows.

tools.name: describe_table
tools.desc: Returns the column names and types of one named table. No cell values.

tools.name: read_query
tools.desc: Returns the rows matching a read-only SELECT the caller writes, up to 100. Nothing changes.

tools.name: insert_row
tools.desc: Inserts one new row into a named table.

tools.name: write_query
tools.desc: Runs an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE the caller writes. DDL is blocked; there is no rollback.

assets.name: publications
assets.desc: Published papers and citations — title, venue, year, DOI, status. Only unreleased pre-print status is sensitive.

assets.name: table-metadata
assets.desc: Column names and types for one table; schema only, no values.

assets.name: projects
assets.desc: The internal project register — project code, title, status, the lead researcher and start date.

assets.name: datasets
assets.desc: Pre-publication research data and its provenance — name, description, classification, size, owner and creation date.

assets.name: employees
assets.desc: Staff records, one row per person — name, email, role, department and salary.

assets.name: api_keys
assets.desc: Stored service credentials, one row per service — the key itself and its owner. One row is independently usable against another system.

assets.name: api_keys
assets.desc: Stored service credentials, one row per service — the key itself and its owner. One row is independently usable against another system.

assets.name: employees
assets.desc: Staff records, one row per person — name, email, role, department and salary.

assets.name: grants
assets.desc: Funding awards — sponsor, grant number, lead researcher, amount, dates and status. A tampered row misstates a sponsor commitment.

assets.name: database-records
assets.desc: What an unrestricted query returns: the caller names the table, so this reaches whatever the credential can see.

assets.name: table-catalog
assets.desc: The list of table names. No cell values, but the names map which systems CBG integrates with and where the credentials live.
